rv.q: Overall the production works like a bleakly amusing charm and, for those who’ve not seen the play before, it’s a treat.
But I never felt Bird's Philip was in touch with despair (as I did, say, when Simon Russell Beale played the part) – that this don's life was a full one and an empty one.

Mr Hampton’s script has some subtle gems (savour the line ‘I just came back to tell you why I wasn’t coming back’) but it is so sparing in its comical crests that even experienced actors might struggle.
Callow’s production neither solves this problem nor plumbs depths in the piece that would make this revival worthwhile.
Yet everyone sounds irredeemably middle-aged in Simon Callow’s stilted production (complete with a cringe-inducing comic curtain call).
This is one of the most misguided revivals you’re likely to see on stage this year, seemingly intent on sabotaging itself at every step.
The production, brilliantly directed by Simon Callow, is exquisite to look at.
This production fails to mount a case.
Simon Callow's direction is seriously underpowered, and at times Libby Watson's gorgeous set holds one's attention rather more than it should.
I really struggle to think of anyone who'd enjoy this revival of Christopher Hampton's desperately dated and unfunny comedy, played ineptly by woefully, inexperienced and ill equipped performers.
What should have been an intellectual firework is here a damp squib.

cn.t: Hampton's clever 1970 comedy gets a misguided revival with weak direction from Callow and TV actors struggling to translate to stage, resulting in a lifeless production that buries the play's wit.
